recent_activity.text: "Yesterday: Arena Hall deep tech tour: a bus, 40 builders and investors, and a 60-mile loop through Starlink → Boring → Black's BBQ → Proto-Town → Oklo's first nuclear reactor. The equation I see: Austin as the dynamic cosmopolitan city engineers want to live in. Land that is lightly regulated, easy to permit, has great utilities, and is low cost. Spirit of Texans: hard working subcontractors, lawmakers who clear pathways, pastors and rabbis who shepherd their flocks... all sitting together over BBQ and beers to say: let's build--for Texas, for America, for the world. 5 things I can't stop thinking about. — 1/ Boring isn't 20% better. It's 10x better. Vegas tendered a project to connect their convention centers. Runner-up bid: $500M. Boring delivered, fully operational: $45M. They're now boring 60 miles under Vegas. And the tunnels are the wedge — not the business. Same playbook SpaceX used to make Starlink possible: cut the cost of the underlying thing, then build everything that becomes economic on top of it. — 2/ Proto-Town is becoming a civil society, not just a campus. A common tool shop. Bunk-bed conversations between engineers from different companies. A speakeasy called the Pink Poodle Club. Limestone arriving for the first synagogue — Josh Kushner is delivering the Torah. Another founder is financing a church, where they'll host music nights and Sunday worship. This is what early SpaceX and early Neuralink felt like. Neuralink built robots above a bar. Boring was digging holes with no roof. Velocity comes from trust + proximity + shared tools. — 3/ The American Shenzhen — minus the parts we'd never copy. No forced labor. No human rights violations. No state-owned enterprises. Yes co-located manufacturing, shared specialty equipment, housing next to the lab, and regulators who say yes. Jacob DeWitte (Oklo) walked us through a small modular reactor built in ~230 days. Same project in Idaho: 3+ years. — 4/ The unsung infrastructure is a man named John Cyrier. 25-year Caldwell County resident. Former elected official. Built and sold a construction company. Knows hundreds of subs in Central Texas. He wasn't a \"nice to have.\" He was load-bearing. He has the relationships and trust--much needed and deserved. — 5/ The ecosystem is the product. Starlink's head of production told us their hardest hire isn't engineers. It's specialty trades who'll relocate to Austin — because if Starlink stops needing them tomorrow, there's no second customer. The fix: more atoms-economy companies in the same zip code. Re-industrializing America is a real thing. It's happening in Central Texas."

"America has settled into a deserved 2nd place in most areas of competition, often behind China. But there is a framework for hope. Last week, I had the honor of emceeing Endless Frontiers. The question we kept circling: what is \"Remember the Alamo\" for this generation? A bit of Texas history. After months of crushing defeats, Sam Houston had no reason to be an optimist. Then on April 21, 1836, during the Mexican Army's afternoon siesta, he launched a surprise attack and won the war in 18 minutes — paving the way for Texas independence and American continental power. So what's our \"Remember the Alamo\" today? Three from history: → Sputnik (1957). A Soviet beach ball in orbit gave us DARPA, NASA, the National Defense Education Act, and a generation of moonshots. → Mountain Pass. America discovered rare earths. Molycorp, our champion, went bankrupt in 2015 after Chinese subsidies undercut it. The Pentagon now buys F-35 magnets from China. → Desert One (1980). Eight helicopters into Iran. Sandstorms, mechanical failures, a collision on the ground, eight Americans dead. That humiliation built modern SOCOM, Delta Force, and the 160th SOAR. Former Office of Net Assessment Director Jim Baker added contemporary ones: → The War on Terror — 20 years, $8 trillion, 7,000+ American dead, no strategic gains → The 2008 Financial Crisis — 6 million families lost their homes; no banker prosecutions → COVID — worst per-capita death rate among advanced democracies; half a year of schooling lost → The Afghanistan withdrawal — 11-day collapse, 13 Marines dead at Abbey Gate → The opioid crisis — hundreds of thousands dead, an inadequate response I'd add three more that haunt the industrial base: → U.S. shipbuilding — China builds about half the world's ships. We build less than 1%. → Bell Labs — the greatest corporate R&D engine in human history, dismantled. → The 155mm shell — when Ukraine asked for artillery, our industrial base couldn't keep up. So where's the hope? Tocqueville nailed it 200 years ago. When the French want something, they demand it of the bureaucrats. When the British, the aristocrats. When Americans want something, they simply do it. That voluntary self-organization explains everything from the VFW to garden clubs, the Rotary to the Elks Lodge. When former DNI Avril Haines was asked whether anything like that is happening in China right now, she answered: \"Absolutely not.\" What's happening here — at this conference and in this country — is people from different industries, professions, and ideologies self-organizing to understand our defeats, plot strategy, and steel themselves to do hard, important things. We may be #2 in synthetic biology, quantum, humanoid robotics, university research, and even national approval. We remain #1 at self-organizing, collaborating, and executing. There is no better moment to inject more of that spirit as we begin the next 250 years. #EndlessFrontiers #AmericanRenewal #Reindustrialization"

recent_activity.text: Happy official birthday to KNIX! 13 years ago today we launched with an Indiegogo crowdfunding campaign and an article in the Toronto Star entitled "Panty firm targets new moms". I started Knix with a dream to help the 1 in 3 women that deal with light bladder leaks. It was a problem no one wanted to talk about, with language that didn't exist yet and a product that many people thought sounded gross. It's hard to believe that 13 years later we have created an entirely new category. That 1 in 2 menstruating teens in the US now wear leakproof underwear and what was once considered taboo is now mainstream. Building a company takes a village and the Knix team is simply incredible. Every day they bring their hard work, passion, belief and friendship to help shape and build Knix into the company it is today. There are so many things to be proud of over the past 13 years but the Knix team is by far the standout.

recent_activity.type: Ann Crady Weiss shared a post
recent_activity.text: "I started Hatch in the nursery. I never expected we’d be the top item on Gen Z’s wishlist. But that's the story Ali Donaldson tells in today's Inc. Magazine piece. Over the last few years, we noticed young adults gravitating toward Hatch on TikTok and leaned into it. This generation, the one that my children are a part of, want something different on their nightstand than a phone. We made sure Hatch could deliver. Today, we’re in seven million homes. We're a sleep brand for every stage of life — newborns, toddlers, adults, and Gen Z alike. What I'm most proud of isn't just the cultural moment. It's what's underneath it: a company with $200M in revenue, built on $37M raised. Low churn. High daily engagement. A business that compounds because people actually come back to it, every single night. That doesn't happen by accident. It happens when you stay close to your customer, make hard calls early, and follow what the market is actually telling you, even when it surprises you. Thank you to Ali Donaldson at Inc., to Toni Schneider and Erin Merani for lending their voices to this story, and to the entire Hatch team who makes all of it possible. Read the full article here: https://lnkd.in/gaq8KvRJ"

recent_activity.text: "Trust takes time. We've spent over a decade building trust with parents and caregivers at Once Upon a Farm, and we're not willing to sacrifice that trust for the sake of speed. One thing you can count on: we're never going to rush a product to market if it doesn't meet our brand standards for taste, nutrition, and safety. Our Refrigerated Oat Bars are a perfect example. These took two years to develop because we wanted a drizzle that looked and tasted great, and we weren't willing to compromise by adding sugar to it. I'm so proud of our final result. And for years, families had been asking us for meat baby food and more protein-forward options. It took a huge cross-functional team effort to perfect these recipes, our positioniong and to source organic meat we truly felt good about. And yes, I still personally taste-test every single snack and meal we create! That extra time and effort to get it right is worth it every time."
